Definition: Whether an official government web portal or mobile application exists where taxpayers can file tax returns and pay taxes online with direct e-payment capability linked to instant payment system.
Comments: Value=3 (Under development). Government announced rollout/development of the e-KORI system (online tax filing and payment platform) in Jan 2026, with phased implementation, indicating the tax portal is under development rather than already fully operational nationwide.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original comment only checked the new e-KORI project (launched as an implementation phase 19 Jan 2026, World Bank-backed, phased rollout). However, OBR's own website confirms a pre-existing operational portal ('Umutangakori'/Télédéclaration-Télépaiement) already provides online tax declaration and e-payment, with user guides for bank-account activation and online filing/payment. Since an operational e-filing + e-payment portal already exists (with e-KORI as a further modernisation under development), the code is revised up to 4=Yes.

Comments: Value=2 (Yes). BRB-operated RTGS/ATS and bank transfer rails support business payments; UNCDF report describes RTGS/ACH and interbank transfer systems, which are standard channels used for business-to-business transfers.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Value=4 (Partially functional). Burundi participates in regional payment arrangements through BRB’s RTGS-related regional linkages; UNCDF notes Burundi is an EAPS member (since 2020) with integration incomplete as of Oct 2022 and REPSS integration pending, indicating some cross-border capability via regional systems but not fully integrated/complete.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: BRB's own May 2026 article on payment interoperability states that joining PAPSS (the continental instant cross-border system) is still the 'next logical step' and that BRB is 'invited to finalise' this integration — i.e. not yet joined. The 2022 EAPS/REPSS SWIFT-based integration was still 'being tested' per UNCDF and no evidence of completion since. No operational cross-border instant payment corridor is confirmed as of mid-2026, so the code is revised down to 3=Under development rather than 4=Partially functional.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: Value=2 (Limited use). Humanitarian and government-related cash transfer programs have used mobile money rails in Burundi; GSMA describes UNHCR delivering mobile money-enabled cash assistance to Burundian returnees via Lumicash, indicating G2P-like digital transfer usage but not comprehensive nationwide government benefit digitization.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited 2020 GSMA source concerns a UNHCR (not government) pilot for returnees, which is weak evidence of G2P. A far stronger and current source (World Bank, May 2026) documents the government-led Merankabandi social protection programme, implemented by the Ministry of National Solidarity via the CORE-MIS digital platform and mobile money, reaching over 1 million people and used to disburse shock-response payments to 100,000+ households during 2025/26 floods. This shows active, government-run digital G2P disbursement at meaningful scale, so the code is revised up to 3=Yes-Active Use.

Comments: Value=2 (General data protection legislation). Burundi’s parliament adopted a new legal framework regulating collection and use of personal data (public and private sectors) and creating an independent oversight authority (January 2026).

Burundi's National Assembly adopted the bill unanimously on 15 January 2026 (own website) and it was promulgated as Loi n°1/03 du 10 mars 2026 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (confirmed via ARCT, the telecoms/ICT regulator). It is a general data protection law (not payment-specific) with an independent oversight authority. Value unchanged at 2=General Data Protection Legislation.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Value=2 (Partial). Burundi’s National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS) 2015–2020 was developed through a participatory process and explicitly prioritizes underserved groups (rural population, women, youth, micro and small entrepreneurs) as priority clienteles, indicating inclusion intent but not necessarily formal representation in payment-system governance bodies.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited NFIS 2015-2020 (drafted 2014) is now expired; its NFIS Coordination and Monitoring Committee did include multi-stakeholder representation (banks, insurers, consumer/transparency association ABUCO-TI, farmers' groups). A March 2026 workshop validated successor national financial-inclusion and financial-education strategies (SNIF/SNEF) with government, financial institutions and civil society participation, supported by IFAD. This is broader financial-inclusion governance rather than payment-system-specific governance, so evidence still only supports Partial; value unchanged at 2, but the year/sourcing should be updated to reflect the 2026 validation rather than the stale 2015 document. Flagged for human review to confirm whether BurundiPay's own governance/scheme body has a distinct consumer-representation mechanism.

Since the operating rules for the national instant payment system are openly downloadable, the code is revised up to 3=Yes-Fully Public.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing an instant/real-time payment system (IPS/RTP) that enables digital payments with near-instant settlement (typically within seconds), available 24/7/365. This includes both bank-led and mobile money interoperability systems.
Comments: Value=4 (Partially deployed). Burundi has operational core interbank infrastructure (RTGS/ACH/CSD) owned/maintained by BRB and a national retail payments switch (Bi-Switch) that supports interoperability across ATMs/POS, but retail interoperability is incomplete (only 9/14 commercial banks and 2/41 MFIs connected in 2022; mobile money operators Ecocash and Lumicash were still in testing integration).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Materially updated evidence: BRB officially launched a genuine 24/7 instant payment system, 'BurundiPay' (ISO 20022-based), on 23 April 2026, Burundi's 22nd such system in Africa, supporting bank accounts and mobile wallets including USSD access. As of the BRB press briefing on 6-7 May 2026, only 3 banks (Interbank, Finbank, BCAB) and 8 microfinance institutions had fully integrated, with other institutions still finalising integration and full onboarding targeted for completion by ~5 September 2026. This confirms the system is operational nationally but participant integration is still incomplete, so the code remains 4=Partially deployed, now on stronger, current, primary-source evidence rather than the 2023-vintage UNCDF assessment.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: Value=3 (Yes). GSMA documents UNHCR delivering mobile money-enabled cash assistance to Burundian returnees and notes Lumitel obtained Central Bank approval to accept a temporary certificate as valid identification to register/activate Lumicash accounts, evidencing accommodations to enable migrant/returnee access to mobile money under KYC rules.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with better sourcing. A regional refugee financial-inclusion study and a UNHCR Burundi country report both confirm Burundi has no specific mobile money regulation, but in practice the refugee ID card (issued by ONPRA) or the 'attestation de rapatriement' is accepted as sufficient identification to open a mobile money account, corroborating the original GSMA-sourced finding with more specific and durable evidence. Value unchanged at 3=Yes, though access rests on practice rather than codified regulation — worth noting in future updates.
